lead: A physical defect is a short, an open or a missing implant. There are too many shapes and sizes to test one by one, so test programs work on a small logical fault list. A fault model maps a defect onto a line stuck at 0 or 1, two bridged lines, or a path that is too slow. The stuck-at model is the workhorse; delay faults catch chips that compute the right value too late. Fault simulation and ATPG in 6.3 depend on this list.
prereq: You need Boolean gates and truth tables (Unit 3) and gate-level Verilog modelling (Unit 5); the fault list built here is used by fault simulation and ATPG.

sections.h3: From physical defect to logical fault

blocks.text: A defect is physical: a metal short, an open contact, a missing implant, a thin oxide pinhole. A fault is the logical abstraction of that defect: for example, line A is stuck at logic 0. An error is a wrong signal value somewhere inside the circuit. A failure is a wrong value at an output pin during a test. A short from an input of a NAND gate to ground may behave like that input stuck at 0.

A defect has a size, a resistance and a location; its effect changes with all three. A fault model fixes the effect, not the cause. The single stuck-at model assumes one line is fixed at 0 or 1 while every other line works. The list is finite, so a program can enumerate it, generate vectors and report fault coverage.

A line is a primary input, a primary output or a gate terminal. A line stuck-at-0 (SA0) always reads logic 0. A line stuck-at-1 (SA1) always reads logic 1. Single means only one line is faulty at a time.

blocks.where: N<sub>SA</sub> is the number of single stuck-at faults; L is the number of lines; the factor 2 is for SA0 and SA1.

blocks.text: Two faults are equivalent if no input vector can tell their faulty outputs apart. On a two-input NAND gate, A/0, B/0 and Z/1 all force the output to 1 for every input, so they form one equivalence class. A/1 and B/1 are not equivalent: A/1 changes the output only when B=1, and B/1 changes it only when A=1.

Fault collapsing keeps one fault per equivalence class. If every test for fault g also detects fault f, then f dominates g; drop f because testing g covers it. With fanout, a stem fault is equivalent to the multiple fault in which every fanout branch is stuck at the same value, so test programs place checkpoints on the fanout branches and do not count the stem again. A redundant fault has no vector that detects it; ATPG identifies such faults and they are excluded from the fault list before fault coverage is computed.

A transistor stuck open never conducts; a transistor stuck short always conducts. In static CMOS, a stuck-open may disconnect the output from the positive supply (VDD) or from ground for one input combination. The output then holds its old value on load capacitance. Detection may need two vectors: the first sets the output to 0, the second tries to drive it to 1. If the transistor is open, the output stays at 0.

A bridging fault shorts two lines. If one driver pulls 0 and the other pulls 1, the result depends on drive strength. It is often modelled as wired-AND (0 wins) or wired-OR (1 wins). A resistive bridge may pass logic tests but add delay.

A transition delay fault makes one line slow-to-rise or slow-to-fall. A path delay fault makes a whole input-to-output path too slow. The test uses a vector pair and two clock edges: the first vector sets the line to its initial value, the launch clock edge creates the transition, and the capture clock edge captures the response after the rated clock period. If the path is too slow, the captured value is the old one.

examples.question: A two-input NAND gate has inputs A, B and output Z. (a) List every single stuck-at fault. (b) Collapse the faults into equivalence classes. (c) Give the smallest test set that detects at least one fault from every class. Write each vector as (A,B).
steps: The gate has three lines: A, B and Z. Number of single stuck-at faults is 2 × 3 = 6: A/0, A/1, B/0, B/1, Z/0, Z/1.
A/0 forces A=0, so Z=1 for all B. It differs from the good gate only at 11. B/0 does the same. Z/1 also forces Z=1 for all inputs. So {A/0, B/0, Z/1} is one equivalence class.
A/1 forces A=1. It differs only at (0,1), where good Z=1 but faulty Z=0. B/1 differs only at (1,0). They are separate classes.
Z/0 forces Z=0. It differs at 00, 01 and 10. It is a separate class. Total classes: 4.

Class {A/0,B/0,Z/1} needs vector 11. A/1 needs 01. B/1 needs 10. The set {01,10,11} covers all four classes with 3 vectors. 00 detects Z/0 alone, but 01 and 10 already detect Z/0, so 00 is not needed.
examples.answer: The 6 single stuck-at faults collapse to 4 equivalence classes, and the smallest test set is {01, 10, 11}, which has 3 vectors.
examples.check:
import itertools
vectors=[(0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)]
def nand(a,b):
    return 0 if (a==1 and b==1) else 1
faults=[('A/0','A',0),('A/1','A',1),('B/0','B',0),('B/1','B',1),('Z/0','Z',0),('Z/1','Z',1)]
def out(name,line,val,a,b):
    if line=='A': a=val
    if line=='B': b=val
    z=nand(a,b)
    if line=='Z': z=val
    return z
sigs={}
for f in faults:
    name,line,val=f
    sig=tuple(1 if out(name,line,val,a,b)!=nand(a,b) else 0 for a,b in vectors)
    sigs.setdefault(sig,[]).append(name)
classes=list(sigs.keys())
min_size=None
for r in range(1,5):
    for combo in itertools.combinations(range(4),r):
        if all(any(sig[i] for i in combo) for sig in classes):
            min_size=r
            break
    if min_size is not None:
        break
print(len(faults))
print(len(classes))
print(min_size)

traps: On a two-input NAND, Z/1 is equivalent to A/0 and B/0; it is not a separate class.
A/1 and B/1 are not equivalent on a NAND; each is detected only when the other input is 1.
Single stuck-at means one line at a time, not all lines at once.
A stuck-open in CMOS can escape a single-vector test; it often needs a two-vector sequence because the floating output keeps its old value.
A delay fault test needs a launch edge that creates the transition and a capture edge after the rated period; testing only the final logic value misses a slow path.

quiz.q: Define stuck-at-0 and stuck-at-1 for a line.
quiz.a: SA0: the line always reads logic 0. SA1: the line always reads logic 1. Single stuck-at means only one line is faulty at a time.

quiz.q: Why can two different stuck-at faults be equivalent?
quiz.a: For every input vector they produce the same faulty output at the primary outputs, so no test can tell them apart.

quiz.q: A 3-input NAND gate has inputs A, B, C and output Z. How many single stuck-at faults exist?
quiz.a: There are 4 lines: A, B, C and Z. Number of faults = 2 × 4 = 8.

quiz.q: For the two-input NAND example, which vector detects A/1 and what output difference appears?
quiz.a: Vector (A,B)=01. Good Z=1; with A stuck at 1, Z=NAND(1,1)=0.

quiz.q: Why may a stuck-open transistor in a CMOS gate need two vectors?
quiz.a: The open disconnects the output for some input. The first vector charges the output node to a known value; the second tries to drive it to the opposite value. If the transistor is open, the node stays at the old value, so the fault is seen only as a sequence.

quiz.q: Why are redundant faults removed from the fault list before computing fault coverage?
quiz.a: No input vector can detect them. Keeping them would make 100% coverage impossible even for a correct design.

quiz.q: State the difference between a transition delay fault and a path delay fault.
quiz.a: Transition delay fault: one line is slow to rise or slow to fall. Path delay fault: a complete input-to-output path is too slow, even if each gate is within its own limit.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry adds cell-aware fault models, and FinFET defects make some opens and shorts behave differently from planar CMOS. Delay test is run at-speed on automatic test equipment, and path selection is a research problem. Search for cell-aware ATPG, transition delay test, and path delay fault coverage.
